source_read: PDF, JAMA 2006;295:2003–2017, all 15 pages (text layer read in full; Figure 1 on p. 2005 and Tables 2–9 with Figures 2–4 on pp. 2009–2014 checked on rendered pages; pp. 2016–2017 are mostly group lists and references)

claims.overstatement: None in what the claim attributes to COMBINE. The trial's own result runs against the claim's headline association (role contradicts) and the claim reports it as such. No medicine dose or regimen in the statement or magnitude.
claims.note: As far as this source goes: COMBINE was a US, outpatient trial at 11 academic sites, double-blind for medication, and found no benefit of acamprosate on either coprimary outcome, on time to first drink, or in the year after treatment, so 'both in the US and one of them COMBINE, found no benefit' is right. COMBINE prints no counts of return to any drinking by arm (only that time to first drink showed no significant effect), so its contribution to the review's pooled risk difference, and whether it had 'by far the most events', cannot be checked from this paper. COMBINE numbers in the magnitude: 78.4 against 77.6, P=.61, and HR 0.85 (0.63 to 1.15) are as printed. The magnitude's caveat that the main-effect HR's basis is unclear is borne out by the editors' interval-width calculation (anchor on p. 2010); the pooled proportions with a heavy drinking day were 69.6% against 70.1%. Comparison group: placebo acamprosate (half of them on naltrexone), pooled over CBI. Diarrhoea in COMBINE: 65% against 35% (printed; 193/303 against 108/309), at a higher daily dose than most earlier trials (study condition), a larger excess than the review's 11 in 100. COMBINE was NIAAA-funded but ran under the manufacturer's investigational licence with donated medicines and manufacturer site monitoring.

anchors.locator: Abstract › Design, Setting, and Participants; Results; Conclusions
anchors.extracted: Randomized trial, January 2001 to January 2004, of 1,383 recently abstinent volunteers (median age 44) with DSM-IV primary alcohol dependence at 11 US academic sites, 16 weeks of outpatient treatment. No significant effect of acamprosate on drinking compared with placebo, whether given alone or combined with naltrexone and/or CBI; the authors conclude there was no sign that acamprosate worked, with or without CBI.

anchors.locator: Results › Study Population, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: In the 30 days before randomization only 2.3% had been medically detoxified and 7.7% had had inpatient treatment; at randomization 42% had been abstinent for 4 days, 24% for 5 to 7, 18% for 8 to 14 and 15% for 15 to 21. So COMBINE participants were mostly not recruited after inpatient detoxification, unlike the trials the claim describes as the majority.

anchors.locator: Table 3 (Main Effects, Acamprosate row; Interactions, Acamprosate × naltrexone and Acamprosate × CBI rows); Results › Within-Treatment Drinking Outcomes for Pill-Taking Groups › Primary Outcomes, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Adjusted mean percent days abstinent over the 16 weeks: acamprosate 78.4 (SD 25.31; n=605) against placebo acamprosate 77.6 (SD 25.32; n=616), P=.61 (least-squares means adjusted for site and baseline percent days abstinent, model with all main effects and interactions). No significant interaction involving acamprosate (with naltrexone P=.74; with CBI P=.84; 3-factor interaction not significant).

anchors.locator: Figure 2 (Main effects, Acamprosate); Table 4 (Main Effects, Acamprosate row)
anchors.extracted: Acamprosate against placebo: Cohen d for percent days abstinent 0.02 (97.5% CI −0.11 to 0.15); time to first heavy drinking day HR 0.85 (97.5% CI 0.63 to 1.15); at least one heavy drinking day during treatment 423 of 608 (69.6%) against 433 of 618 (70.1%), P=.23 (proportional hazards model). Editors' calculation: the HR interval's log width (0.60) is about √2 times that of the cell-against-cell comparisons in the same figure (0.42 to 0.44, about 300 per cell) and equals what two single groups of about 150 would give (0.60, from 108 and 115 events), not the 0.31 expected for about 610 against 610; so the printed main-effect HR probably compares acamprosate with placebo only within the reference groups of the other two factors.

anchors.locator: Results › Within-Treatment Drinking Outcomes for Pill-Taking Groups › Secondary Outcomes, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: The authors note that abstinence is the primary end point of most acamprosate trials and examined time to first drink as a secondary outcome: no main effect or interaction was statistically significant. No estimate or count of people who returned to any drinking is printed by arm.

anchors.locator: Table 2 (Diarrhea; Withdrawals due to adverse events)
anchors.extracted: By medication group (pooled over CBI): diarrhoea 193 of 303 on acamprosate (printed 65%) and 165 of 305 on acamprosate plus naltrexone (56%) against 108 of 309 on placebo (35%), overall P<.001; withdrawals due to adverse events 9 (3%) on acamprosate against 4 (1%) on placebo, overall P=.09. Same direction as the claim's diarrhoea and drop-out findings; the diarrhoea excess (about 29 to 30 points) is far larger than the pooled 11 in 100. Editors' check: several printed percentages exceed count over column n (193/303 = 63.7%, 165/305 = 54.1%, 92/309 = 29.8% printed 31%), so smaller, unstated denominators were used.

anchors.locator: Comment, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: The authors found the null acamprosate result unexpected in view of many earlier positive trials and list differences: a higher daily dose than in most trials (study condition); COMBINE needed just 4 abstinent days, mostly achieved as outpatients, while most positive trials began after longer abstinence in inpatient care; the earlier trials also assessed less often, used non-standard counselling and recruited mainly inpatients from clinical services.

anchors.locator: Table 7 (Main Effects, Acamprosate row); with Table 8 (Main Effects, Acamprosate row), p. 2014
anchors.extracted: Year after treatment: adjusted mean percent days abstinent 65.0 (n=563) on acamprosate against 65.8 (n=567) on placebo acamprosate, P=.85; at least one heavy drinking day in that year 485 of 608 (79.8%) against 498 of 618 (80.6%), P=.40 (Table 8). COMBINE shows no after-treatment difference on the outcomes it reports (return to any drinking after treatment is not reported).

anchors.locator: Funding/Support; Role of the Sponsors
anchors.extracted: Funded by NIAAA cooperative agreements and career awards; acamprosate, naltrexone and matching placebos donated by Lipha Pharmaceuticals; the trial ran under Lipha's investigational new drug application for acamprosate, and Lipha monitored the sites but took no part in data management, analysis, interpretation or the manuscript. Bears on how the reviews classify this trial's funding.

claims.overstatement: No causal overstatement and no drinking amounts or medicine doses. The headline 'did not detectably change drinking' is stricter than the source: it rests on main effects that the authors say must be read with caution because of the naltrexone × CBI interaction, the authors read the results as CBI helping when naltrexone was not given, and in the preplanned comparison of the two groups on both placebos CBI was nominally better (79.8 against 73.8, P=.04); the claim reports the cell values, so it is not misleading, but this P=.04 comparison is missing. 'In the year after treatment the differences shrank' overstates the fading (see note).
claims.note: Numbers checked on the tables and figures: 1,383; 11 sites; 2001–2004; 4 to 21 days; up to 20 sessions; 9 visits; 78.2 against 77.8 (P=.82); d 0.01 (−0.12 to 0.14); HR 0.81 (0.60 to 1.10); 77.1, 80.6, 79.2, 75.1 (P=.009); d 0.22 (0.03 to 0.40), 0.17 (−0.02 to 0.35), 0.07 (−0.11 to 0.25); 74, 71, 74 against 58; NNTs 6, 7, 7 as printed; 66.6 against 73.8 and 79.8; 61.4, 66.2, 66.6, 67.3 (P=.27); 66.9 against 63.8 (P=.08); power 0.40 to 0.50: all as printed. Not supported: 'In the year after treatment the differences shrank' — the gaps from the placebo-naltrexone/no-CBI cell were 4.8 to 5.9 points after treatment against 2.0 to 5.5 during it, and the CBI main-effect gap grew from 0.4 to 3.1 points; what disappeared was the interaction (the combination no longer lagged). Suggested: 'the pattern changed and none of the differences was clear'. The abstract describes the year-after differences as about the same size but no longer significant, the Results say their direction remained, and only the Comment says they mostly faded. Reference groups: the four percent-days-abstinent cells and the three d values are against placebo naltrexone without CBI, each cell pooled over acamprosate and its placebo (half of each cell took active acamprosate; all had medical management); 'placebo pills alone' and 'naltrexone alone' in the statement should say so, as the magnitude does. The 58, 74, 71 and 74 good-outcome figures are single groups without acamprosate, as labelled. Smaller points: the CBI-only group had four health checks with a health professional (p. 2006), so 'without any pills or medical visits' is not exact ('without pills or medical management'); cannabis and nicotine use disorders were not exclusions, and the exclusion window was the last 90 days (6 months for opioids); median CBI attendance was 10 sessions. The HR caveat is borne out by the editors' interval-width calculation, and the pooled proportions with a heavy drinking day (70.0% with CBI against 69.7% without, Table 4) would be worth adding. Missing data for the good clinical outcome: the printed 1,294 conflicts with the row's own counts (which imply 1,137); either way more than for the coprimary outcomes, as the claim says.

anchors.locator: Abstract › Design, Setting, and Participants; Interventions; Results
anchors.extracted: Randomized trial, January 2001 to January 2004; 1,383 recently abstinent volunteers (median age 44) with DSM-IV primary alcohol dependence at 11 US academic sites. Eight groups had medical management with naltrexone, acamprosate, both or placebos, with or without CBI, for 16 weeks; a ninth had CBI without pills; follow-up to 1 year after treatment. Percent days abstinent 80.6 (naltrexone, n=302), 79.2 (CBI with placebos, n=305) and 77.1 (both, n=309) against 75.1 (placebos and medical management only, n=305); naltrexone × CBI interaction P=.009. CBI without pills or medical management 66.6 (n=157) against 73.8 (n=153) and 79.8 (n=156), P<.001. The abstract adds that a year after treatment these group differences were of about the same size but had lost significance.

anchors.locator: Methods › Recruitment and Randomization, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Recruited by advertisements and clinical referrals (about 5,000 screened). Eligibility: DSM-IV alcohol dependence by structured interview, 4 to 21 days of abstinence, and recent heavy drinking (thresholds as study conditions). Exclusions: DSM-IV abuse or dependence of other substances except nicotine and cannabis in the last 90 days (6 months for opioids) or by urine drug screen; a psychiatric disorder needing medication; unstable medical conditions. Permuted blocks of 9, stratified by site. So people with cannabis or nicotine use disorders were not excluded.

anchors.locator: Methods › Assessment, 1st paragraph (continues on p. 2005); blinding sentence in the 1st paragraph on p. 2006
anchors.extracted: Drinking came from structured interviews (timeline follow-back). At the 9 medical management visits, drinking and craving were assessed by research assistants who knew the psychosocial assignment (and did not deliver it); 2-hour assessments at weeks 8 and 16 and at weeks 26, 52 and 68. Blinding covered medication assignment only (participants and all site staff, through the end of follow-up; p. 2006).

anchors.locator: Methods › Treatment Conditions › Medical Management and Combined Behavioral Intervention paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Medical management: 9 sessions (weeks 0, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 16) by licensed health professionals (14 physicians, 28 nurses, 1 physician assistant, 1 pharmacist); first visit about 45 minutes, later ones about 20; advice to abstain, medication education, an adherence plan, encouragement of mutual-help groups. CBI: up to twenty 50-minute sessions by licensed behavioural health specialists with at least a master's degree, combining cognitive behavioural therapy, 12-step facilitation, motivational interviewing and support-system involvement. The CBI-only group could see health professionals at weeks 4, 8, 12 and 16 for liver tests and health advice.

anchors.locator: Methods › Statistical Methods, 4th paragraph of the section (power)
anchors.extracted: Coprimary end points each tested at a Bonferroni-corrected P=.025 (97.5% CIs; 3rd paragraph, p. 2006). Power above 0.90 for a 10% main effect of each treatment, but estimated power for an interaction half the size of the main effects only about 0.40 to 0.50; the steering committee chose reliable main effects over power for interactions.

anchors.locator: Results › Adherence in Behavioral Interventions (continues on p. 2008)
anchors.extracted: Median sessions completed: 10 for CBI (of up to 20) and 9 for medical management; therapists' adherence ratings median 6 on 7-point scales; mutual-help (AA) attendance during treatment 17% to 35% across groups.

anchors.locator: Results › Biological Verification of Drinking
anchors.extracted: Percent carbohydrate-deficient transferrin fell 15% from baseline to week 16 in those reporting complete abstinence (n=212) and rose 5% in those reporting any drinking (n=694), P<.001: a partial check on self-reported drinking.

anchors.locator: Table 3 (Main Effects, CBI row); Results › Within-Treatment Drinking Outcomes for Pill-Taking Groups › Primary Outcomes, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Adjusted mean percent days abstinent over 16 weeks: CBI 78.2 (SD 25.52; n=614) against no CBI 77.8 (SD 25.36; n=609), P=.82; least-squares means adjusted for site and baseline percent days abstinent, from a model with all main effects and 2- and 3-factor interactions. The authors caution that, given the naltrexone × CBI interaction, the CBI and naltrexone main effects cannot be read on their own. Editors' check: the four no-CBI groups in this analysis total 607 in Figure 1 (153+152+154+148), not 609.

anchors.locator: Table 3 (Interactions, Naltrexone × CBI row); Results › Primary Outcomes, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: All four cells had medical management and each is pooled over acamprosate and its placebo: placebo naltrexone without CBI 75.1 (n=305), naltrexone without CBI 80.6 (n=302), placebo naltrexone with CBI 79.2 (n=305), naltrexone with CBI 77.1 (n=309); interaction P=.009. Abstinent days were lowest without either naltrexone or CBI, and adding CBI to naltrexone brought no further gain. Editors' check: the cell sizes are sums of an acamprosate group and a placebo-acamprosate group (153+152, 154+148, 154+151, 155+154), so half of each cell took active acamprosate.

anchors.locator: Figure 2 (Main effects, CBI); Table 4 (Main Effects, CBI row)
anchors.extracted: CBI against no CBI: Cohen d 0.01 (97.5% CI −0.12 to 0.14); HR for time to first heavy drinking day 0.81 (97.5% CI 0.60 to 1.10); at least one heavy drinking day during treatment 433 of 619 (70.0%) with CBI against 423 of 607 (69.7%) without, P=.16. Editors' calculation: the d interval's width (0.26) is what about 610 against 610 gives, but the HR interval's log width (0.61) is about √2 times that of the cell comparisons (0.43) and equals what two single groups of about 150 with 111 and 115 events give (0.60), against 0.31 for the pooled arms; so the printed main-effect HR most likely compares the two groups on both placebos, with and without CBI.

anchors.locator: Figure 2 (Naltrexone × CBI interaction rows; comparison group placebo naltrexone/no CBI); Results › Primary Outcomes, 3rd paragraph (pp. 2009–2010)
anchors.extracted: Against placebo naltrexone without CBI: d 0.22 (97.5% CI 0.03 to 0.40) for naltrexone without CBI, 0.17 (−0.02 to 0.35) for CBI without naltrexone, 0.07 (−0.11 to 0.25) for both; HRs 0.78 (0.63 to 0.97), 0.84 (0.68 to 1.05) and 0.91 (0.74 to 1.13). For time to heavy drinking the interaction P was .15; only naltrexone without CBI reached significance against the reference, and the other two pointed the same way.

anchors.locator: Results › Within-Treatment Drinking Outcomes for Pill-Taking Groups › Secondary Outcomes, 1st and 3rd paragraphs (3rd continues on p. 2011)
anchors.extracted: Drinks per drinking day (P=.03), drinks per day (P=.03) and heavy drinking days per month (P=.006) all showed a significant naltrexone × CBI interaction, consistent with the coprimary end points. GGT and %CDT did not differ between treatments.

anchors.locator: Results › Clinical Significance; Table 5 (Good clinical outcome row)
anchors.extracted: Good clinical outcome (abstinence or moderate drinking without problems, as defined in Statistical Methods) at end of treatment: 58% placebo with medical management, 74% naltrexone, 71% placebo with CBI, 74% naltrexone with CBI, all with medical management; naltrexone × CBI interaction P=.02. In Table 5 these are single groups without acamprosate: 71 (58.2%), 87 (73.7%), 92 (71.3%), 99 (74.4%). NNTs as printed: 7 for CBI, 6 for naltrexone, 7 for both. Editors' calculation: single groups give NNTs of 6.5, 7.6 and 6.2; cells pooled over acamprosate give 6.0, 7.5 and 6.9; neither reproduces 6, 7, 7 with one rounding rule.

anchors.locator: Table 5 (Good clinical outcome row, No. column); Figure 4 (p. 2012)
anchors.extracted: The row prints 1,294 people with data, but its counts and percentages imply 116 to 133 per group, 1,137 in all (editors' calculation); Figure 4's odds ratios against placebo naltrexone without CBI (1.82, 95% CI 1.26 to 2.65; 1.93, 1.33 to 2.80; 2.16, 1.46 to 3.20) are reproduced exactly from these implied numbers pooled over acamprosate (150/252, 185/254, 196/265, 178/234). So about 18% (246 of 1,383) lacked this outcome, against 0.5% (7 people) for percent days abstinent (1,376 with data) and none for heavy drinking (1,383, missing counted as relapse).

anchors.locator: Results › Within-Treatment Evaluation of CBI Therapy Without Pills (Placebo Effect) › Percent Days Abstinent (continues on p. 2012); Table 5 (Percent days abstinent row)
anchors.extracted: Percent days abstinent during treatment: CBI without pills or medical management 66.6 (n=157), placebo with medical management 73.8 (n=153), placebo with medical management and CBI 79.8 (n=156); overall P<.001; post hoc tests corrected for multiple comparisons: CBI alone against placebo with medical management P=.03, and against placebo with medical management and CBI P<.001.

anchors.locator: Results › Within-Treatment Evaluation of CBI Therapy Without Pills (Placebo Effect) › Percent Days Abstinent (continues on p. 2012)
anchors.extracted: In this preplanned secondary analysis the two groups on both placebos with medical management differed by CBI: 79.8 with CBI against 73.8 without, P=.04 after correction for multiple comparisons, a nominal benefit of CBI when no active medicine was given (not tested at the trial's .025 level for primary analyses).

anchors.locator: Results › Within-Treatment Evaluation of CBI Therapy Without Pills › Relapse to Heavy Drinking; Global Clinical Outcome
anchors.extracted: At least one heavy drinking day: 79.0% with CBI alone against 71.2% with placebo, medical management and CBI (HR 0.77, 97.5% CI 0.60 to 1.00, P=.05); placebo with medical management 75.2%, not significantly different from either. Good global outcome 60.6% (CBI alone), 58.2% (placebo, medical management) and 71.3% (placebo, medical management, CBI), overall P=.07.

anchors.locator: Table 7 (Main Effects and Naltrexone × CBI rows); Results › Posttreatment Follow-up Outcomes › Percent Days Abstinent, p. 2012
anchors.extracted: Year after treatment: abstinent days fell in all groups; cells (with medical management, pooled over acamprosate) 61.4 (n=280), 66.2 (277), 66.6 (287) and 67.3 (286); interaction P=.27; CBI main effect 66.9 (n=573) against 63.8 (n=557), P=.08; naltrexone 66.7 against 64.0, P=.42. The Results say the direction of the during-treatment differences remained but the interaction was no longer significant; CBI alone 60.9, placebo with medical management 59.4, plus CBI 67.5, P=.08 (Table 9). Editors' calculation: the gaps from the placebo-naltrexone/no-CBI cell were 4.8, 5.2 and 5.9 points after treatment against 5.5, 4.1 and 2.0 during it, and the CBI main-effect gap grew from 0.4 to 3.1 points: what disappeared was the interaction, not the size of the differences.

anchors.locator: Comment, 1st paragraph; 4th paragraph (continues on p. 2014)
anchors.extracted: The authors' reading: within medical management, in the absence of CBI naltrexone helped and "without naltrexone, CBI helped"; the combination did not improve outcomes further; given medical management, outcomes were much the same with CBI alone, naltrexone alone or both. They note that all pill-taking participants also had 9 medical management sessions, which may have left little room for the combination to add anything, and that CBI differs from standard cognitive behavioural therapy (more emphasis on AA).

anchors.locator: Comment, 8th paragraph
anchors.extracted: The authors: the between-treatment differences of the treatment period partly persisted but mostly faded during the following year; naltrexone's lower relapse to heavy drinking after treatment was only marginally significant; some indication of more abstinent days after CBI. This is the wording the claim's 'shrank' follows; it differs from the Results text and the abstract (see the Table 7 anchor).

anchors.locator: Comment, 9th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Internal validity described as high (balance at baseline, adherence, complete 16-week drinking data for 94%, biological check of self-report); limits to generalizability: intensive research assessments (up to 12 hours), academic rather than primary-care settings, exclusion of people with substantial psychiatric illness or drug use, and only 16 weeks of treatment.

anchors.locator: Funding/Support; Role of the Sponsors; Financial Disclosures (begin on p. 2015)
anchors.extracted: NIAAA cooperative agreements and career awards; medicines and matching placebos donated by Lipha Pharmaceuticals, under whose investigational new drug application for acamprosate the trial ran (site monitoring by Lipha, no role in analysis or manuscript). Several authors (including Anton, O'Malley, Ciraulo, Johnson, Mason, Pettinati, Swift and Weiss) reported consulting fees, honoraria, grants or research support from drug companies, among them Lipha, Forest and Alkermes.

key_findings.correction: Clarification, not an error: the four year-after values (61.4, 66.2, 66.6, 67.3) are the naltrexone × CBI cells pooled over acamprosate (n = 280, 277, 287, 286; Table 7), all with medical management, as KF 6 says for the treatment-period cells; 'placebo + MM 61.4' follows the paper's own text (p. 2012).

Re-found blind (denominators 122, 118, 130, 116, 129, 133, 125, 132, 132; sum 1,137; Figure 4 reproduced from the pooled cells 150/252, 178/234, 185/254, 196/265). Addition: the pooled cells give NNTs of 6.0, 7.5 and 6.9, closer to the printed 6, 7 and 7 than the single groups (6.5, 7.6, 6.2), so the printed NNTs, like the odds ratios, probably come from the cells pooled over acamprosate, while the text's 58%, 74%, 71% and 74% are the single groups.
Checked on the rendered Table 1 (p. 2008): CBI-only OCDS 18.9 (SD 9.98), P=.47; recomputed F(8, 1374) = 12.5.

Recomputed: from the 97.5% interval, HR 0.77 (0.60 to 1.00) gives z = 2.29, P = .022; read as a 95% interval, P = .045. CBI main effect 0.81 (0.60 to 1.10) gives P = .12 against the printed .16 (the printed P may test the averaged main effect while the HR is a single-cell contrast, per reporting issue index 0).
Checked: the row sums to 974 against 983 in the other rows; Table 9 gives 126 + 122 = 248 (79.7%).
Re-found blind: 115 + 111 = 226 from Table 5; the other cells of the row reproduce exactly.
Re-found blind (e.g. 193/303 = 63.7% printed 65%; 165/305 = 54.1% printed 56%); serious events in Table 2 total 53 against 70 in the text.
Re-found blind: Figure 1 gives 153 + 152 + 154 + 148 = 607; the other main-effect rows of Table 3 total 1,221, the CBI row 1,223.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2, overall some concerns, agreed; domain judgments agreed (medication contrasts at low risk in the first four domains; the CBI and no-pill contrasts rest on self-report by participants and assessors who knew the psychosocial assignment; basis of the main-effect hazard ratios unclear).

interpretation_gap.note: Rating 'substantial' agreed, with two corrections. (1) results_show says that in the year after treatment the differences shrank: not borne out for percent days abstinent; the gaps from the placebo-naltrexone/no-CBI cell were 4.8, 5.2 and 5.9 points after treatment against 5.5, 4.1 and 2.0 during it (Tables 3 and 7; editors' calculation), and the CBI main-effect gap grew from 0.4 to 3.1 points (P=.08); what disappeared was the interaction, and none of the differences met the trial's threshold. (2) Gap (1) should add that on the composite good-outcome measure (secondary) all three arms differed from placebo (odds ratios 1.82 to 2.16, 95% CIs excluding 1; Figure 4) and the preplanned comparison of the two all-placebo groups favoured CBI (79.8 against 73.8 abstinent days, P=.04), which gives the abstract's 'fared better' some support beyond the coprimary end points.

missed: Year after treatment (Table 7, p. 2013, against Table 3, p. 2009): the differences between the four naltrexone × CBI cells kept their size (4.8 to 5.9 points from the reference cell, against 2.0 to 5.5 during treatment) and the CBI main-effect gap widened from 0.4 to 3.1 points (P=.08). The abstract's description (differences of about the same size but no longer significant) fits Table 7; the Comment's statement that the effects largely dissipated (KF 17, p. 2015) overstates the fading for this outcome.

Authors' reading of CBI (Comment, 1st paragraph, p. 2013): within medical management, CBI helped when naltrexone was not given and naltrexone helped when CBI was not given; worth a key finding next to KF 6, because the claim on talking therapy rests on the main effect, which the authors say must be read with caution given the interaction (Primary Outcomes, 2nd paragraph, p. 2009).

Acamprosate (Comment, 2nd paragraph, p. 2013): the authors' explanations of the null result (outpatient start after as little as 4 abstinent days, against longer inpatient abstinence and inpatient recruitment in most positive trials; less frequent assessment and non-standard counselling in earlier trials; a higher daily dose as a study condition) are in the replication timeline but not in a key finding; the acamprosate claim uses this contrast.
